extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and substantive standards for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. Focused on how examiners should analyze original, new, and amended claims to determine whether the specification demonstrates that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement — purpose and separation from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 requires that the 'specification shall contain a written description of the invention * * *.' This requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objectives include: (1) clearly convey that the applicant has invented the subject matter claimed; (2) put the public in possession of what the applicant claims; and (3) describe the technology being patented. Case citations: Vas-Cath, Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle, Capon v. Eshhar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency standard — possession by one skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the written description requirement, a patent specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry is fact-based and varies depending on the nature of the invention. Mere allegations of possession are insufficient (Enzo Biochem). Relevant cases: Moba B.V. v. Diamond Automation; Vas-Cath; Enzo Biochem.

rubrics_metrics.name: How an applicant shows possession (descriptive means)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant shows possession of the claimed invention by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using descriptive means such as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be demonstrated by actual reduction to practice, showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. (Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposits of biological materials — limited role
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference in the specification to a deposit of biological material made in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may satisfy the written description requirement with respect to a claimed material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deposit is not a substitute for written description; the written description of the deposited material needs to be as complete as possible because examination proceeds on the written disclosure. Deposits made after filing generally cannot support additions or corrections to the original disclosure; see 37 CFR 1.804 and MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong presumption for original claims
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO/examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims. Rejection of an original claim for lack of written description should be rare (In re Wertheim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claims — essential/critical feature must be described
rubrics_metrics.description: Even for original claims a lack of adequate written description may arise if an aspect or an essential/critical feature of the claimed invention has not been described with sufficient particularity so that one skilled in the art would recognize applicant had possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim requires an essential feature not adequately described in the specification and that feature is not conventional or known in the art, the claimed invention as a whole may not be adequately described (example: 'A gene comprising SEQ ID NO:1' where promoters, enhancers, coding regions, etc., may be insufficiently described).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-only disclosures and correlation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention described solely in terms of a method of its making coupled with its function, without a described or art-recognized correlation between structure and function, normally is not a sufficient identifying characteristic for written description purposes (especially for biomolecule sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional characteristics must be coupled with a known or disclosed correlation to structure to be sufficient. Software is an exception where disclosure of functions may suffice because writing code is within the skill of the art (Fonar). For biomolecules, a function-only disclosure typically fails (In re Bell, In re Deuel examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/species disclosure — requirement to 'reasonably lead' to species
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad or 'laundry list' disclosure of every possible moiety does not constitute a written description of every species in a genus because it would not 'reasonably lead' those skilled in the art to any particular species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be sufficient disclosure to reasonably lead to the claimed species; generic disclosures do not necessarily support a claimed subgenus or species. Case examples: Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, Purdue Pharma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on new matter for new or amended claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The proscription against the introduction of new matter in a patent application (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251) prevents adding information that goes beyond the subject matter originally filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement. The original claims are part of the disclosure; applicants may amend the specification to include claimed subject matter if originally present (In re Benno). See MPEP §2163.06–.07.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for added claim limitations — express, implicit, or inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly added claim limitations must be supported in the specification through express, implicit, or inherent disclosure; an amendment to correct an obvious error may be permissible if one skilled in the art would recognize the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With sequence data, corrections for sequencing errors may be possible if the application included sequence information and referenced a deposit; deposits made after filing generally cannot support additions unless accompanied by a compliant 37 CFR 1.804 statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of disclosed 'essential' limitation can defeat written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation that the specification describes as essential or critical to the invention may mean the inventor did not possess the broader claimed invention, and such a claim may fail the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification makes clear that a particular narrow understanding of a claim term is an 'essential element' and variations are outside the inventor's stated purpose, omitting that element in a claim can render the claim unsupported (Gentry Gallery, Tronzo examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner methodology — read and analyze the specification; examiner initial burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should read and evaluate the entire application; the examiner has the initial burden, after a thorough reading and evaluation, of presenting evidence or reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize that the written description provides support for the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant should point out support for any amendments; if the examiner finds disclosure does not reasonably convey possession, the examiner must present evidence or reasoning explaining why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — determine what each claim as a whole covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; consider the preamble, transitional language, and claim body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble language can be structural and part of the claimed invention; transitional terms ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') have specific meanings and affect scope. For searching/applying prior art, 'consisting essentially of' may be construed as 'comprising' absent a clear specification definition of what materially changes basic and novel properties (see PPG).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review entire application to find support for each element/step
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to determining compliance, the examiner should review the claims and the entire specification including embodiments, figures, and sequence listings to understand how applicant provides support for the various features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether an element is critical to show possession; determine the field of the invention and the level of skill in the art. Generally, the higher the skill/knowledge in the art, the less specificity required; well-known information need not be described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of adequate written description — reduction to practice and other evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice, detailed drawings, structural chemical formulas, sufficiently detailed identifying characteristics, or combinations thereof that would allow a skilled artisan to recognize inventor had possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice provides strong evidence but is not necessary in every case; disclosures such as restriction maps, isolation of mRNA and expression data, or detailed structural formulas can be adequate depending on the subject matter. Case citations: Cooper, Pfaff, Vas-Cath, Eli Lilly, Enzo Biochem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biomolecule-specific identifying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: For some biomolecules, identifying characteristics that can demonstrate possession include a sequence, structure, binding affinity, binding specificity, molecular weight, and length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural formulas and deposits are convenient methods, but other characteristics may suffice. Example: an antigen fully characterized by structure, formula, chemical name, physical properties, or deposit may provide adequate written description for an antibody claimed by binding affinity; conversely, an antibody claim defined by binding affinity to an inadequately described antigen fails (Noelle v. Lederman).

rubrics_metrics.name: No per se requirement for examples or recited structure for biological macromolecules
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no per se rule that an adequate written description of an invention involving a biological macromolecule must contain a recitation of known structure or specific examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are not necessary; the written description standard may be met even where actual reduction to practice is absent. Courts have held that novel combinations of known segments (chimeric genes) can meet written description without reiterating structure if disclosure conveys possession (Falkner v. Inglis; Capon v. Eshhar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess disclosure-to-claim scope correlation from skilled artisan viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must compare the scope of the claim with the scope of the description from the standpoint of one of skill in the art at the filing date to determine whether applicant demonstrated possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes determining whether the disclosure reasonably conveys possession of the invention as now claimed, taking into account field-specific knowledge and what is conventional in the art. The inquiry is case-by-case and factual (Vas-Cath; In re Smith).
